item.title: Pros4D: Modeling Evolving 4D Worlds in Latent Space for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 41% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Rongxin Gao, Dongxuan Liu, Chu Li, Chengyang Ji, Jialing Huang, Runyu Chen, Kairun Wen, Chenxin Li, Jingrui Ye, Haosong Zhen, Xinghao Ding, Yue Huang, Yuzhi Huang, Xiaotong Tu, Jingyan Jiang
arXiv:2611.19803v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.

item.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
item.description:
Relevance: 39% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang
arXiv:2611.27689v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

item.title: ReactDrive: Self-Reactive Driving World Model
item.description:
Relevance: 38% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yifan Wang, Xiaoqi Wang, Cho-Ying Wu, Wenbin He, Chenyu You, Liu Ren
arXiv:2611.27024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .

item.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
item.description:
Relevance: 37% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Chengchao Lv, Yin Wang, Chunzheng Zhu, Wanli Chang
arXiv:2611.27780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

item.title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
item.description:
Relevance: 37% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, You Wu, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
arXiv:2611.27166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.

item.title: From Reflection to Co-Evolution: Self-Evolving Agents with Locally Verified Memory
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xinxiang Yin, Xinglang Zhang, Haodong Chen, Zhiqing Cui, Weidong Tang, Yuxuan Wang, Junrui Wang, Jingyi Zhang, Jianfeng Zhang, Jian Qian
arXiv:2611.10382v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents have made impressive progress in coding and mathematical reasoning, motivating growing interest in learning from long-horizon interaction. Memory supports this process, but plausible lessons can be redundant or reinforce inappropriate actions. Can a memory's source decision provide a practical test for whether to retain it? We localize consequential trajectory steps, extract candidate memories, and replay each source decision with and without its candidate under the same context. This reveals two properties: most candidates barely shift the probed distribution, and both successful and failed source actions can be reinforced or suppressed. These observations motivate Anchor, which tests shift magnitude and source-role alignment before retention. Admitted memories guide later trajectories, enabling experience-driven improvement under a frozen policy. On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, Anchor improves success rate and mean score by up to 19.9% and 17.2%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline for each backbone. With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld cards than unfiltered retention and outperforms all four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.

item.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Hexiang Wei, Jiajin Wu, Juelin Li, Mingjian Liang, Fan Yang, Zhuowei Liang, Zihao Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Lin Shao
arXiv:2610.39278v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://roboscience-ai.github.io/worldflow-page/.

item.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xianzhe Fan, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Jing Wang, Yecheng Wu, Yu-Cheng Chou, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Jan Kautz, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Zhiding Yu, Hengshuang Zhao, Zhiqi Li
arXiv:2611.25105v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

item.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Maximilian Seeth, Chengzhi Martin Hu, Marie Kempkes, Paul R\"ottger, Leo Schwinn
arXiv:2611.26296v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill$.$png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill$.$png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill$.$png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

item.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mateo Cl\'emente, George Z. Xue, Amin Abyaneh, Liheng Ma, Rui Heng Yang, Tongtong Cao, Zhanguang Zhang, Yingxue Zhang
arXiv:2611.08156v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $\pi_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

item.title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Sunli Chen, Yun Zong, Qinhong Zhou, Xiaowen Qiu, Jiaben Chen, Zeyuan Yang, Chuang Gan
arXiv:2611.27182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

item.title: See, Remember, Explore: A Benchmark and Baselines for Streaming Spatial Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
arXiv:2603.23864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spatial understanding is fundamental for embodied agents, yet most spatial VLMs and benchmarks remain offline-evaluating post-hoc QA over pre-recorded inputs and overlooking two crucial deployment-critical requirements: long-horizon streaming inference and active perception when the current view is insufficient. To address this gap, we introduce S3-Bench, a benchmark suite for streaming spatial question answering with active exploration, where queries are temporally grounded to specific timestamps and must be answered using only observations available up to that moment. S3-Bench adopts a dual-domain design, combining a scalable simulator with controllable trajectories and exploration actions, and real-world streaming videos that capture practical sensing artifacts for rigorous generalization evaluation. Overall, it spans 10K+ scenes and 26K+ trajectories, with dedicated training (S3-Train) and evaluation (S3-Eval) splits. We further propose AMF-VLM, which supports streaming spatial reasoning under bounded computing via (i) memory folding, which compresses long-horizon observations into compact structured memory, and (ii) active exploration, which outputs explicit actions (e.g. move/rotate/scan) to acquire missing evidence before answering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared to models using identical training data, our approach yields improvements of 8.8% and 13.3% on the simulated and real splits of S3-Eval, respectively, while maintaining competitive transferability to standard spatial benchmarks.

item.title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mingxuan Wang, Siyuan Du, Yanfeng Wang, Ya Zhang, Chencheng Zhang, Jiangchao Yao
arXiv:2611.27427v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

item.title: Towards Embodied Air-Ground Cooperative Object Search: Benchmark, Dataset and Agentic Method
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Boao Yu, Zimo Chen, Junreng Rao, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Yong Zhao, Jianzhe Gao, Pengfei Zhu, Rusheng Ju
arXiv:2609.08402v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Urban object search, locating a specific object from a single reference image without route or direction instructions and confirming the instance up close, is a fundamental capability for embodied agents. Existing urban embodied benchmarks evaluate one segment of this chain: navigation ends at a coordinate, and detection and question answering stop at an answer. We present AGOS-Bench, the first benchmark for urban cooperative object search by an air-ground team, integrating aerial discovery and ground-level instance verification in one closed loop. Nine metrics assess search, cooperation, and verification, and they distinguish "found but unconfirmed" from "never found". AGOS-Dataset instantiates the task in 2,125 episodes across six city maps under seen and unseen test settings, contributing 27,720 Train Examples along with 1,100 Expert Trajectories. To solve the task, we propose AGOS-Agent, which combines algorithmic coverage and approach routing with event-driven MLLM judgments for target verification and cooperation. On the unseen test set, zero-shot AGOS-Agent (Qwen3.5-4B) achieves a success rate (SR) of 37.67%, 7.00 percentage points (pp) above a controlled baseline with identical information, actions, and prompts. LoRA fine-tuning raises SR to 57.00% (+19.33 pp). Adapted existing systems AGC-VLN-OS and AeroDuo-OS achieve SRs of 31.33% and 28.67%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/Yomier/AGOS-Bench.

item.title: ViewDreamer: A Robot World Model beyond Fixed Camera Setups
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
arXiv:2611.26981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.

item.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Changin Choi, Jungwon Park, Jungmin Ko, Jimyeong Kim, Wonjong Rhee
arXiv:2611.27381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

item.title: Spatial Query Execution as Verifiable Rewards for Multi-step Spatial Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jiyoon Pyo, Dongwon Jung, Zekun Li, Nayeon Kim, Muhao Chen, Yao-Yi Chiang
arXiv:2611.26787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.

item.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Maximilian Rokuss, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Alejandro Lozano, Benjamin Hamm, Yannick Kirchhoff, Fabian Isensee, Klaus Maier-Hein
arXiv:2611.27876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

item.title: SiMDex: Mining Similar Egocentric Videos for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Nie Lin, Takehiko Ohkawa, Sijin Chen, Ruoshi Wen, Zhuohang Li, Liqun Huang, Zhengming Zhu, Yiming Bao, Yunfei Li, Minjie Cai, Xiao Ma, Wei Xu, Yoichi Sato
arXiv:2608.04196v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent years have witnessed an explosive trend of scaling ego-centric human videos for robot manipulation, yet it remains unclear which data actually benefits dexterous manipulation. We present SiMDex, a similarity-based data mining framework that casts human data selection for VLA post-training in dexterous manipulation as a recommendation problem. For each robot demonstration, SiMDex runs a recall-ranking-re-ranking cascade over ~32M egocentric human samples: two stages, recall and ranking, select a task-relevant subset in a morphology-agnostic action space, and re-ranking verifies it on pixels, with no change to VLA architecture or training. Against a strong baseline trained with an equal amount of randomly sampled human data, SiMDex uses only ~1.49M mined samples (<5% of the pool) yet improves the overall success rate from 47.7% to 61.7%, showing that selective curation outperforms indiscriminate data mixing.

item.title: TrajRealm: A Large-Scale Point Tracking Dataset with Diverse Dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ni Yang, Weiguang Zhao, Jiafei Cao, Yankai Jiang, Haoyu Guo, Tao Yang, Chunhua Shen, Junting Dong
arXiv:2611.27136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

item.title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making in Signed Networks
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Vishnudatta Thota, Aditi Saxena, Twinkle Tripathy, Vaibhav Srivastava
arXiv:2611.27147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.

item.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala
arXiv:2611.27641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

item.title: 2D or 3D? Rethinking Token Pruning in 3D VLAs with Cross-Modal Correlation Awareness
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zihao Zheng, Zhihao Mao, Quanyou Li, Hangyu Cao, Sicheng Tian, Lingyue Zhang, Chenyue Li, Ziyun Zhang, Hong Gao, Yuchen Huang, Yutong Xu, Guojie Luo, Xiang Chen
arXiv:2604.09244v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D vision-language-action (VLA) models process both image and point cloud tokens at each control step, increasing the cost of action prediction. Token pruning can reduce this cost, but a token's contribution depends on which other tokens remain. We present 2Dor3D, a framework that jointly selects which 2D and 3D tokens to retain under a fixed token budget. Our analysis shows that either modality can compensate for the other within a patch, that neighboring correlations help explain differences in pruning risk, and that shared tokens couple pruning decisions across patches. In one box-closing observation, two patches with nearly identical interaction scores differed eightfold in the action deviation caused by removing their image token. Guided by these findings, 2Dor3D transfers cross-modal prediction residuals to retained tokens, uses neighborhood correlation entropy to explore more retention choices at local outliers, and updates pruning costs after each proposed exchange between coupled regions. A fused GPU kernel packs the selected tokens into a shorter sequence for subsequent Transformer layers. Across RLBench and LIBERO, 2Dor3D speeds up end-to-end inference by $2.06$--$2.10\times$ on MLA and $1.86$--$1.91\times$ on FiS-VLA, with task success rates 0.5--0.6 percentage points below the corresponding unpruned models.

item.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
arXiv:2611.27124v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.

item.title: UniEvo-VL: An On-policy Self-Distillation Training Recipe for Multimodal Model Self-improvement
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Fang Wu, Da Xing, Ji Wang, Yanjie Huang, Junxi Wang, Hejia Geng, Guancheng Wan, Bowen Zuo, Xiaomin Li, Shixiang Tang, Xinyu Xiang, Zehong Wang, Shiyi Du, Peng Xia, Shuangjia Zheng, Yining Hong, Li Erran Li, Jure Leskovec, Yejin Choi
arXiv:2609.38721v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern multimodal models bring generation and understanding into a single unified system, which enables them to provide and learn from their own feedback. Motivated by this unified capacity, we introduce UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute. Instead of relying on a separately trained, stronger generator as teacher, we use critiques of the generator's own outputs, produced by a fixed vision-language critic, as privileged information. The generator and its EMA copy act as student and teacher under different contexts. The student only sees the vanilla question, while the teacher conditions on the privileged critique. Then training minimizes the per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions over the student's own sampling trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that UniEvo-VL improves the image generation capabilities of multimodal models, while maintaining their sensitivity to additional reflection information. With Qwen-Image-2512, direct-generation performance improves from 0.747 to 0.808 on GenEval using Qwen feedback and from 32.97 to 35.53 on GenEval2 Soft-TIFA using the external Luna critic. Moreover, attempts with more powerful external critics (e.g., GPT5.6-Luna) show that multimodal models with strong judge capabilities can anticipate a higher self-evolving ceiling. Last but not least, mixed text-rendering outcomes show that our self-improvements may not be uniform across different tasks. Our study aims to shed light on the current hot recursive self-improvement research line to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without paired ground-truth images, human annotation, or task-specific reward functions.

item.title: PhysForce: Physics-aware Force Control for Interactive Video World Model
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xuancheng Xu, Xiaofeng Wang, Yue Ma, Zheng Zhu, Bing-Kun Bao
arXiv:2611.27164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model's internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.

item.title: WAM-Sim0.1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jiahao Cui, Jiaye Li, Wenhao Zhang, Yaoyi Li, Shan Luan, Quanhui Tang, Jianhua Han, Lin Cheng, Hang Xu, Siyu Zhu
arXiv:2611.07939v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. item.title: OpenAHBU: Open-sourced Automatic Human Behaviour Understanding Toolkit Through Facial Behaviour Analysis
item.description:

arXiv:2611.27862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic facial behaviour understanding (AFBU) is fundamental to various human-centred applications, yet existing academically available toolkits offer limited functionality, closed training pipelines, and weak generalisation. This paper presents OpenAHBU, a fully open-sourced, generalisable toolkit integrating 11 AFBU functions across three semantic levels: (i) short-term external facial attributes, including landmarks, blendshapes, Action Units, and expressions; (ii) short-term facial behaviour-related human psychological states, including valence/arousal and pain; and (iii) long-term facial behaviour-related psychological traits, including depression and personality. More importantly, models of most functions are trained on a comprehensive corpus aggregating multiple academically available datasets, ensuring robust cross-dataset generalisability.In addition, we include a Synergistic Multi-task Enhancement (SMTE) module to efficiently and adaptively enhance each OpenAHBU function by leveraging the complementary cues contained in its most-related support function's predictions.Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our OpenAHBU outperformed existing open-source toolkits not only in functional coverage but also the predictive performances, while providing superior deployment flexibility across diverse computational scenarios.With fully publicly available training and inference scripts, pre-trained weights, user-friendly GUI, Python library, and cross-platform compatibility, our OpenAHBU provides a reproducible, scalable and extensible toolkit at https://github.com/OpenAHBU/OpenAHBU.

item.title: EgoLAM: Learning Latent Actions from Hand and Head Motion
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ziyi Ding, Yiwei Wang, Zhongxing Wei, Xianxin Lai, Yechi Liu, Xiaodi Huang, Jinghua Hou, Xiaoquan Sun, Haijier Chen, Zhe Liu, Yinan Chen, Junqiao Zhao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Jiayu Chen
arXiv:2611.27290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.

item.title: Learning Interaction Dynamics via Motion-Region Guidance for Robotic Video World Models
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
arXiv:2611.27344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.

item.title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shengxiang Xu, Liang Yao, Shuyi Chen, Yishu Wang, Shimin Di, Fan Liu, Bishun Yao, Hanghui Guo, Xinyu Liu, Chengye Liang, Yuyu Luo, Min-Ling Zhang
arXiv:2611.27110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

item.title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Caoyuan Ma, Wendi Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Muyao Niu, Yujie Lu, Zengxi Zhang, Ji Zhao, Shuai Dong, Wenpu Liu, Ziyue Wang, Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Haiyuan Wan, Xuehui Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Wenqi Shao, Yinqiang Zheng
arXiv:2611.27467v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. item.title: MoHA: Model-Conditioned Harness Adaptation for Long-Video Agents
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jianghan Chao, Wenhui Tan, Hang Su, Qiuyu Tian, Tanxiao Li, Bingzi Zhang, Zequn Liu, Ruihua Song, Yingce Xia
arXiv:2611.27646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. item.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

item.title: Reason in the Words You Speak: Idiolectal Paraphrasing Off-Policy Traces for Reasoning Distillation in VideoLLMs
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ji Soo Lee, Jinyoung Park, Seohyun Lee, Jongha Kim, Joonmyung Choi, Jinsung Yoon, Hyunwoo J. Kim
arXiv:2608.26684v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent large language models achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, where reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has emerged as a leading paradigm for optimizing models on self-generated trajectories. However, the on-policy nature of GRPO bounds the model to the reasoning skills it can already produce, restricting to learn more advanced capabilities. Prior works inject privileged reasoning traces from a stronger teacher policy to guide training, yet these traces are inherently out of distribution with respect to the student policy. We observe that this mismatch between on-policy and off-policy causes gradient clipping on semantically critical reasoning tokens, ultimately rewarding correct answers while leaving the reasoning that justifies them unlearned. Hence, we propose Echo-GRPO, a framework that lets the model reason in the words it speaks. Rather than imitating low-probability privileged traces from the teacher model, Echo-GRPO rewrites them into the student policy's own idiolect, that is, its own characteristic vocabulary and expression patterns, while preserving their semantics via Dual-Reference Decoding. We instantiate this framework as VideoEcho-R1 for video reasoning distillation, achieving consistent improvements across three multimodal LLM backbones and five benchmarks. Finally, we show that our idiolectal paraphrasing is a plug-in module that consistently improves both RL and supervised fine-tuning frameworks for reasoning distillation, demonstrating that policy-aligned supervision extends beyond GRPO.

item.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Michael W. Spratling, Heiko H. Sch\"utt
arXiv:2611.27811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

item.title: StepX-OPD: Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Chenru Wang, Xuanyang Zhang, Yucheng Han, Wenbo Nie, Wei Cheng, Xianfang Zeng, Gang YU, Chi Zhang
arXiv:2611.04386v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. We introduce StepX-OPD, which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Motivated by a decomposition of the rollout's KL, we also regress the student's velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

item.title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision

arXiv:2611.27264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. item.title: MemLife: Curating and Reasoning over Long-Term Egocentric Video Memories
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Guangzhi Xiong, Xinyuan Zhang, Xiao Yang, Hyokun Yun, Kai Zhang, Shiun-Zu Kuo, Hyeonjeong Ha, Xilun Chen, Kai Sun, Lucas Liang, Guangqiang Dong, Ejaz Ahmed, Ahmed A Aly, Anuj Kumar, Raffay Hamid, Aidong Zhang, Xin Luna Dong
arXiv:2609.40195v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-term egocentric video enables personalized AI assistants to reason about daily life. However, as video histories grow to hundreds of hours spanning months or years, reprocessing raw clips for every query becomes computationally prohibitive. Memory systems offer a scalable alternative by compacting videos into text representations, but often fail on practical benchmarks: either the memory does not preserve key evidence, or the retriever fails to locate relevant entries due to retrieval competition in growing search spaces. To address these challenges, we introduce MemLife, a multimodal memory system that constructs entity-grounded, first-person text episodes and retrieves them via a time-indexed agentic reader. Without training or query-time video access, MemLife improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 4.6-12.0% across four long-horizon benchmarks. To further improve memory quality, we propose MemOpt, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes the memory writer to produce faithful, informative, and retrievable memories. MemOpt consistently improves MemLife by 2.7-5.0% across different video and question distributions, with gains that generalize across writer and reader backbones and memory systems.

item.title: PAWS: A Parametric Model of Canine Pose and Shape
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Theo Wieland, Zala \v{Z}gank, Silvia Zuffi, Ylva Mellbin, Elin Hernlund, Hedvig Kjellstr\"om
arXiv:2611.27720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape. We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

item.title: GenSight: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Juelin Li, Chengzhi Zhao, Hexiang Wei, Lin Shao
arXiv:2610.39232v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.
